lessons.title: Acting a sketch: a quarrel during a game
lessons.objective: Act a sketch built on a familiar scene and show willingness to perform.
lessons.course: A sketch is a short scene acted by a few people. Actors learn their lines, speak loudly, face the audience and show feelings with the face and body. A good sketch on a familiar scene has a problem and a solution.

support.title: Short script
support.text:
NEBA: That was out! The ball went out!
EKANE: No, it was in! You always cheat!
REFEREE (whistles): Stop! I saw it. The ball was in. Neba, accept it.
NEBA (calmer): All right. Sorry, Ekane. Let’s play.
EKANE: Thank you. Well played!

lessons.model: Three adults act the scene: angry voices, the whistle, then calm voices.
lessons.guided: Learn one role and act the sketch. Then change the ending and act it again.
lessons.exercise: Who solves the problem in the sketch?
lessons.remediation: Act the sketch reading the script first.
lessons.transfer: Act the sketch for your family and ask what they learnt.

practice.prompt: Put the lines in order.
What does an actor do to be understood?
choices: speak loudly and face the audience
practice.answer: speak loudly and face the audience
practice.explanation: The audience must see and hear.

practice.prompt: Act the sketch with two partners.

lessons.title: A cartoon strip: the borrowed ball
lessons.objective: Read a cartoon strip, explain the feelings of characters and deduce the moral lesson.
lessons.course: A cartoon strip tells a story in boxes (panels). Speech bubbles show what characters say; thought bubbles show what they think. We read panels from left to right and top to bottom.

support.title: Cartoon strip (four panels described)
support.text:
Panel 1: Tabi borrows Ayuk’s new ball. Bubble: “I’ll bring it back tomorrow.”
Panel 2: Tabi plays near the road and the ball is crushed by a car.
Panel 3: Thought bubble: “Should I hide it?”
Panel 4: Tabi gives Ayuk his savings. Bubble: “I’m sorry. I will buy you another one.”

lessons.model: The adult reads each panel and asks: “What is Tabi thinking? What would you do?”
lessons.guided: Read the strip. Say how Ayuk and Tabi feel in each panel. Draw a fifth panel.
lessons.exercise: What does a thought bubble show?
lessons.remediation: Read only the speech bubbles first.
lessons.transfer: Draw a four-panel cartoon about a game.

practice.prompt: What is the moral of the strip?
choices: Be honest and take care of borrowed things.
practice.answer: Be honest and take care of borrowed things.
practice.explanation: Tabi told the truth and repaired the damage.

practice.prompt: Put the panels in order.
items: Tabi wonders if he should hide it.

practice.prompt: Draw panel 5: what happens next?
practice.answer: A fifth panel with a speech bubble.

lessons.title: Building a paragraph: compound sentences with and, but, so
lessons.objective: Combine simple sentences into compound sentences and build a paragraph about a game.
lessons.course:
A simple sentence has one idea: “We played football.” A compound sentence joins two ideas with a coordinating conjunction: and, but, or, so. “We played football and we won.” “It rained, but we continued.” “I was tired, so I rested.”
A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea. It starts with a topic sentence and ends with a concluding sentence.
lessons.model: The adult joins two sentences with “but” on the board, then writes a five-sentence paragraph about a match.
lessons.guided: Join six pairs of sentences. Then write a paragraph of five sentences about your favourite game.
lessons.exercise: Join with “so”: It was dark. We went home.
lessons.answer: It was dark, so we went home.
accept: It was dark, so we went home
It was dark so we went home
lessons.remediation: Use “and” only first, then add “but” and “so”.
lessons.transfer: Write a paragraph about a game you played this week.

practice.prompt: Choose the right conjunction.
practice.text: I wanted to play, [[but]] it was raining. Bih kicked the ball [[and]] scored.

practice.prompt: Which sentence is compound?
choices: We ran fast, but we lost.
practice.answer: We ran fast, but we lost.

practice.prompt: Write a paragraph of five sentences about your favourite game.
practice.answer: A paragraph with a topic sentence and a concluding sentence.

lessons.title: Adverbs of manner, place and time; interjections
lessons.objective: Use adverbs of manner, place and time, adverbs that modify verbs and other adverbs, and interjections.
lessons.course:
Adverbs tell us how, where or when: manner (quickly, carefully, well), place (here, outside, everywhere), time (now, yesterday, soon). They modify verbs (“She runs quickly”) and other adverbs (“She runs very quickly”).
Interjections express feelings and take an exclamation mark: Hurray! Bravo! Hey! Oh! Hello!
lessons.model: The adult commentates a race: “Ngum runs fast! She runs very fast! Hurray, she wins! Bravo!”
lessons.guided: Commentate a game with five adverbs and two interjections. Sort adverbs into manner, place and time.
lessons.exercise: Which word is an adverb in: “Neba played well.”?
lessons.remediation: Ask “how?” after the verb to find adverbs of manner.
lessons.transfer: Commentate a family game with adverbs and interjections.

practice.prompt: Match each adverb with its kind.
practice.answer: quickly: manner; outside: place; yesterday: time.

practice.prompt: Which interjection shows joy after a goal?
Complete with an adverb that modifies another adverb.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting fractions in a game
lessons.objective: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator and with related denominators.
lessons.course:
Same denominator: add or subtract the numerators: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8; 7/10 − 4/10 = 3/10.
Related denominators: change one fraction first: 1/2 + 1/4 = 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4; 2/3 − 1/6 = 4/6 − 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2.
lessons.model: The adult shares a skipping rope game: Bih jumps for ½ of the time, Ngum for ¼. Together: ¾.
lessons.guided: Use fraction strips to solve six additions and subtractions. Write each answer in its simplest form.
lessons.remediation: Use fraction strips with the same denominator first.
lessons.transfer: Describe a game time with fractions: ½ hour of football, ¼ hour of rest.

practice.prompt: 1/2 + 1/4 = ?/4. Write the numerator.
9/10 − 3/10 = ?/10. Write the numerator.
Which is equal to 1/2?

lessons.title: Measuring angles with a protractor
lessons.objective: Identify right, acute and obtuse angles and measure angles with a protractor.
lessons.course:
An angle is the turn between two lines that meet. A right angle measures 90° (the corner of a book). An acute angle is less than 90°; an obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°. A straight angle is 180°.
With a protractor: put the centre on the vertex, the 0° line on one arm, then read where the other arm crosses the scale.
lessons.model: The adult measures the angle of an open door and of the hands of a clock at 3 o’clock (90°).
lessons.guided: Draw five angles and measure them with a protractor. Name each one: acute, right or obtuse.
lessons.exercise: An angle measures 120°. Is it acute, right or obtuse?
lessons.remediation: Compare each angle with the corner of a book first.
lessons.transfer: Find right angles at home and measure two other angles.

practice.prompt: Match each angle with its kind.
How many degrees in a straight angle?
Where do we put the centre of the protractor?
choices: at the end of an arm
practice.explanation: The vertex is the point where the arms meet.

lessons.title: Quadrilaterals, pentagons and hexagons on the playground
lessons.objective: Differentiate quadrilaterals and identify pentagons and hexagons; construct shapes with local materials.
lessons.course:
A quadrilateral has 4 sides: square, rectangle, parallelogram (two pairs of parallel sides), trapezium (one pair of parallel sides), rhombus (4 equal sides).
A pentagon has 5 sides; a hexagon has 6 sides (like the cells of a honeycomb).
lessons.model: The adult makes shapes with sticks: 4 sticks for a square, 5 for a pentagon, 6 for a hexagon.
lessons.guided: Construct a square, a trapezium, a pentagon and a hexagon with sticks or straws. Count sides and corners.
lessons.exercise: How many sides does a hexagon have?
lessons.remediation: Count the sides by touching them one by one.
lessons.transfer: Find quadrilaterals and hexagons in your environment (tiles, a football).
lessons.materials: Sticks or straws, string or clay.

practice.prompt: Match each shape with its number of sides.
Which quadrilateral has only one pair of parallel sides?
Draw a pentagon and a hexagon.
practice.answer: A five-sided and a six-sided shape.

lessons.title: Order of operations (BODMAS) in game scores
lessons.objective: Carry out calculations involving more than one operation following BODMAS.
lessons.course:
BODMAS gives the order: Brackets first, then Of, Division and Multiplication (from left to right), then Addition and Subtraction (from left to right).
3 + 4 × 2 = 3 + 8 = 11 (not 14). (3 + 4) × 2 = 7 × 2 = 14.
lessons.model: The adult calculates a score: 3 goals of 2 points plus 5 bonus points: 3 × 2 + 5 = 11.
lessons.guided: Solve eight calculations using BODMAS. Explain each step to a partner.
lessons.remediation: Underline the operation to do first in each line.
lessons.transfer: Invent a scoring game with points that need BODMAS.

practice.prompt: What do we calculate first in 8 + 6 ÷ 2?

lessons.title: Electricity: conductors, insulators and safety in play
lessons.objective: Identify conductors and insulators, describe how electrical devices should be used and the dangers of electricity.
lessons.course:
Conductors let electricity pass: metals (copper, iron, aluminium), water. Insulators stop electricity: plastic, rubber, dry wood, glass. Electric wires are copper covered with plastic.
Safety: never touch a socket or a fallen wire, do not use devices with wet hands, do not fly kites near power lines, do not climb electric poles, unplug by holding the plug, not the cable.
lessons.model: The adult shows a cable: “The copper inside carries electricity; the plastic around it protects us.”
lessons.guided: Sort objects into conductors and insulators (spoon, ruler, key, rubber, nail). With a torch battery, a bulb and wires, test which objects light the bulb (with an adult).
lessons.exercise: Is plastic a conductor or an insulator?
lessons.transfer: Check at home with an adult that no cable is damaged.
lessons.materials: Battery, bulb, wires, objects (with an adult).

practice.prompt: Match each object with its kind.
Where is it dangerous to fly a kite?
choices: in an open field far from wires
on the beach far from wires
practice.explanation: The kite can touch the wires.

practice.prompt: Why must we not touch devices with wet hands?
practice.explanation: Wet hands can get a shock.

lessons.title: Je joue au football, j’aime faire du vélo
lessons.objective: Parler de ses sports et de ses loisirs.
lessons.course:
Pour les jeux et les sports : « Je joue au football / au ballon. Je joue à la corde. Je joue aux billes. » (au + masculin, à la + féminin, aux + pluriel)
Pour les goûts : « J’aime nager. J’aime faire du vélo. Je n’aime pas courir. Mon loisir préféré, c’est la danse. »

support.title: Dis avec l’adulte
support.text:
Je joue au handball.
Je joue à la marelle.
J’aime faire du vélo, mais je n’aime pas nager.

lessons.model: Ekane dit : « Le samedi, je joue au football avec mes amis. J’aime aussi dessiner. Je n’aime pas regarder la télévision longtemps. »
lessons.guided: Fais une enquête dans la classe : « Tu joues à quoi ? Qu’est-ce que tu aimes faire ? » Note trois réponses.
lessons.remediation: Travaille d’abord « au football » et « à la corde ».
lessons.transfer: Dis en français ton loisir préféré à ta famille.

practice.prompt: Complète avec au, à la ou aux.
practice.text: Je joue [[au]] basket. Elle joue [[à la]] marelle. Ils jouent [[aux]] billes.
practice.explanation: au + masculin ; à la + féminin ; aux + pluriel.

practice.prompt: « J’aime faire du vélo » veut dire…
Écoute et réponds : Tu joues à quoi ?
practice.listen: Tu joues à quoi pendant la récréation ?
practice.answer: Par exemple : Je joue au ballon.

lessons.title: Solving conflicts in games and staying safe
lessons.objective: Resolve conflicts peacefully, practise safety measures and report suspected people and objects.
lessons.course:
A conflict is a disagreement. To solve it peacefully: stop and calm down, listen to each side, say how you feel without insulting, look for a solution together, ask a mediator (a teacher, a prefect) if needed.
Security: do not touch unknown objects or bags left alone, do not follow strangers, report anything suspicious to an adult at once.
lessons.model: Two pupils argue about a ball. A prefect asks each one to explain, then they agree to take turns.
lessons.guided: Act three conflicts from games and solve them with the steps. Make a poster “If you see a suspicious object…”.
lessons.exercise: What should you do if you see a bag left alone near the school?
lessons.answer: Do not touch it and tell an adult.
accept: do not touch it and tell an adult
Do not touch it and tell an adult
lessons.remediation: Learn the first two steps: stop, listen.
lessons.transfer: Use the steps to solve a disagreement at home.

practice.prompt: Put the steps of solving a conflict in order.

practice.answer: A sentence with I feel… because…

lessons.title: Making a ball from local materials
lessons.objective: Fabricate objects such as a ball and a rope from local materials following given dimensions.
lessons.course:
Local materials: plastic bags, old cloth, banana fibres, raffia, string. To make a ball: roll plastic bags or cloth tightly into a ball, tie it with string in many directions, cover with another layer and tie again until it is round and firm (for example about 20 cm across).
A rope: twist three strands of fibre together.
lessons.model: The adult rolls plastic bags into a ball, ties it and measures it with a tape.
lessons.guided: Make a ball about 20 cm across. Play a passing game with it. Twist three strands into a short rope.
lessons.exercise: About how wide should your ball be?
lessons.remediation: Make a small ball (10 cm) first.
lessons.transfer: Make a ball for a younger child.
lessons.materials: Plastic bags, old cloth, string, tape measure.

practice.prompt: Put the steps in order.
items: Tie again until it is round.

lessons.title: Singing in two parts: a sol-fa round
lessons.objective: Sing following parts with correct pitch and produce music to entertain.
lessons.course:
In a round, groups sing the same tune but start one after the other, so the parts overlap. Each group must keep its own part and listen to the others.
We can practise with sol-fa notes: do – re – mi – do, do – re – mi – do, mi – fa – sol, mi – fa – sol. Group 1 starts; group 2 starts when group 1 reaches the third line.
lessons.model: The adult sings the sol-fa line, then a second adult starts later, showing how the parts overlap.
lessons.guided: Learn the sol-fa round in two groups. Then add a clapped rhythm and perform it.
lessons.exercise: In a round, do all groups start at the same time?
accept: no, they start one after the other
lessons.remediation: Sing the tune all together many times before splitting into groups.
lessons.transfer: Sing the round with your family in two groups.
lessons.materials: None, or a small drum for the beat.

practice.prompt: Put the notes in order: do, …
What must each group do in a round?
choices: keep its own part and listen
practice.answer: keep its own part and listen

practice.prompt: Listen and repeat the line.
practice.listen: do, re, mi, do. do, re, mi, do. mi, fa, sol. mi, fa, sol.
practice.answer: The line sung with correct pitch.
practice.explanation: Each note is a step up.

lessons.title: Volleyball: the dig and the set
lessons.objective: Handle a ball in volleyball, follow the basic rules and identify the roles of the players.
lessons.course:
Volleyball: two teams of six players separated by a net. The ball must go over the net; each team can touch it at most three times before sending it back. It must not touch the ground.
The dig (forearm pass): join the hands, arms straight, hit the ball with the forearms. The set: hands above the forehead, push the ball up with the fingers.
lessons.model: The adult shows the dig and the set, then passes the ball to a child.
lessons.guided: Practise the dig and the set in pairs ten times. Play a small game three against three over a rope.
lessons.exercise: How many times can a team touch the ball before sending it over?
lessons.remediation: Throw and catch over the net first.
lessons.transfer: Play a small volleyball game with friends.
lessons.materials: A light ball, a rope or net.

practice.prompt: How many players are on a volleyball team on the court?

choices: the other team wins the point
practice.answer: the other team wins the point
practice.explanation: The ball must not touch the ground.

lessons.title: A sketch about a traditional game
lessons.objective: Act roles in a sketch based on games and show love for acting.
lessons.course:
Many communities have traditional games: songo (a board game with seeds), hide-and-seek games, wrestling, games with rhythm and clapping. A sketch can show children playing, a disagreement and how an elder helps them.
We act in the family language for some lines, with the help of an adult.
lessons.model: The adult and two children act children playing a seed board game; an elder explains a rule.
lessons.guided: Ask an elder about a traditional game. Act a short sketch about it with some lines in the family language.
lessons.answer: For example: songo, a seed board game.
lessons.remediation: Act the sketch without words first, then add lines.
lessons.transfer: Teach a traditional game to friends.
lessons.materials: Seeds, a board or holes in the ground.

practice.prompt: What can a sketch show?
choices: children playing, a problem and a solution
practice.answer: children playing, a problem and a solution
practice.explanation: A sketch tells a short story.

practice.prompt: Write three lines of your sketch.
practice.explanation: Some lines can be in the family language.

practice.prompt: Act your sketch with partners.

lessons.title: Programming a sprite with Scratch
lessons.objective: Change costumes, backdrops and the size of a sprite and make a sprite say something with Scratch.
lessons.course:
Scratch is a free program to create stories and games by joining blocks. A sprite is a character; a costume is one of its looks; the backdrop is the background. Blocks give instructions in order: “when green flag clicked”, “say Hello! for 2 seconds”, “next costume”, “change size by 10”.
A program is a sequence of instructions that the computer follows exactly in order.
lessons.model: The adult builds a short program: when the green flag is clicked, the cat says “Hello!”, changes costume and grows.
lessons.guided: With an adult, make a sprite greet, change costume twice and change the backdrop. Without a computer, write the blocks on cards and act them.
lessons.exercise: In Scratch, what is a sprite?
lessons.remediation: Use only two blocks: the green flag and “say”.
lessons.transfer: Write the steps of a morning routine as a program of instructions.
lessons.materials: A computer with Scratch (with an adult) or block cards.

practice.prompt: Put the blocks in order.
practice.explanation: A program starts with an event.

practice.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
What does a computer do with a program?
choices: follows the instructions exactly in order
practice.answer: follows the instructions exactly in order
